params.question: What is the primary mechanism by which an obstetric vesicovaginal fistula develops during prolonged obstructed labour?

answers.text: Direct laceration of the bladder wall by the fetal skull during delivery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The fetal skull does not tear through the bladder. The mechanism is sustained compression of the vesicovaginal septum between the skull and the bony pelvis, cutting off blood supply and causing ischaemic necrosis over many hours.

answers.text: Ischaemic pressure necrosis of tissues compressed between the fetal head and bony pelvis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. During obstructed labour, the fetal head traps the bladder base and vesicovaginal septum against the bony pelvis. Hours of compression cut off blood flow, the starved tissue dies, and once the baby is delivered the dead tissue sloughs away, leaving a direct bladder-to-vagina communication.

answers.text: Ascending bacterial infection from the cervix weakening the vesicovaginal septum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Obstetric fistula is a mechanical and vascular injury, not an infectious process. The key factor is sustained ischaemia from prolonged compression, not bacterial invasion.

answers.text: Dehiscence of an episiotomy extending into the bladder wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Episiotomy involves the perineum, not the vesicovaginal septum. Obstetric fistula results from ischaemic necrosis caused by prolonged impaction of the fetal head against the bony pelvis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The mechanism is ischaemic pressure necrosis. The fetal head compresses soft tissues against the bony pelvis for many hours, cutting off blood supply. The tissue dies and sloughs away after delivery, creating the fistula.
Exactly right. The single biggest risk factor is duration — obstructed labour exceeding 24 hours carries the highest risk of ischaemic pressure necrosis.

interactions.label: What is the primary advantage of syndromic management of sexually transmitted in

params.question: What is the primary advantage of syndromic management of sexually transmitted infections over laboratory-confirmed diagnosis in resource-limited settings?

answers.text: It uses fewer antibiotics than pathogen-specific targeted therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Syndromic management actually tends to overtreat, covering multiple possible pathogens for each syndrome. Its advantage lies in immediacy of treatment, not in antibiotic economy.

answers.text: It eliminates the need for clinical examination and risk-factor assessment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Clinical examination is central to syndromic management — the clinician must identify the syndrome pattern and assess risk factors such as partner number, condom use, and partner symptoms to guide the standard regimen.

answers.text: It enables treatment at the very first visit, preventing loss to follow-up

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When lab results take days, many patients never return. Syndromic management closes that window by starting a standard regimen covering all likely pathogens immediately, based on the clinical syndrome and risk factors. Field studies across sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia confirmed this approach reduces STI prevalence without losing the first-visit treatment opportunity.

answers.text: It achieves higher diagnostic specificity than microbiological culture

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Syndromic management sacrifices specificity — some patients receive treatment for infections they do not have. This trade-off is accepted because the consequences of untreated STIs (spread and complications) outweigh the cost of occasional overtreatment.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key advantage is first-visit treatment. In settings where lab results are delayed or unavailable, waiting means patients never return and infections keep spreading. Syndromic management treats immediately based on clinical pattern and risk factors.

Well done. NACO's five core syndromic flowcharts — genital ulcer disease, urethral discharge, vaginal discharge, lower abdominal pain, and inguinal bubo — are built on this first-visit treatment principle.

interactions.label: In genital tuberculosis, the absence of constitutional symptoms such as fever, n

params.question: In genital tuberculosis, the absence of constitutional symptoms such as fever, night sweats, and weight loss effectively rules out the diagnosis.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Constitutional symptoms are absent in the majority of genital TB cases. The disease earns its reputation as a 'silent' infection precisely because it damages the reproductive tract without causing fever or systemic illness. Relying on constitutional symptoms to suspect genital TB would miss most cases — primary infertility is the commonest presentation.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Only a minority of women with genital TB display constitutional symptoms. The disease is characteristically 'silent,' destroying the fallopian tubes and endometrium over months or years without overt illness. The most common presentation is primary infertility, discovered long after the original haematogenous seeding from a healed pulmonary focus.

interactions.label: According to CDC guidelines, which minimum clinical finding justifies initiating

params.question: According to CDC guidelines, which minimum clinical finding justifies initiating empirical treatment for pelvic inflammatory disease in a sexually active woman with no other identified cause?

answers.text: Positive endocervical swab for Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The CDC minimum criteria deliberately do not require laboratory confirmation. Waiting for culture results risks leaving PID untreated, which can cause irreversible tubal damage and infertility.

answers.text: Fever above 38.3 °C together with an elevated white blood cell count

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fever and leucocytosis support the diagnosis in moderate-to-severe cases but are not required. Even subclinical PID without systemic signs causes the same tubal scarring as severe disease.

answers.text: Uterine tenderness, adnexal tenderness, or cervical motion tenderness on pelvic examination

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The CDC deliberately sets a low threshold: any one of these three findings, in a sexually active woman with no other explanation, justifies starting empirical treatment. This is because even the mildest PID causes tubal scarring, and the risk of untreated disease (infertility, ectopic pregnancy) far outweighs the risk of empirical antibiotics.

answers.text: Mucopurulent vaginal discharge with bilateral lower abdominal guarding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While mucopurulent discharge and abdominal signs may accompany PID, they are not required for initiating treatment. The deliberately low minimum threshold — pelvic tenderness alone — exists because subclinical and mild PID cause the same long-term tubal damage as clinically obvious disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: The CDC minimum criteria require only pelvic tenderness — uterine, adnexal, or cervical motion tenderness — without laboratory confirmation. This low threshold exists because even mild, subclinical PID causes permanent tubal damage, and the consequences of undertreatment far outweigh those of overtreatment.

Exactly. Cervical motion tenderness — pain when the cervix is gently moved side to side — is considered the hallmark of PID. The low diagnostic threshold reflects the high stakes of missed or delayed treatment.

params.question: A woman has continuous urinary leakage per vaginam following a hysterectomy. The methylene blue dye test is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?

answers.text: Vesicovaginal fistula with a very small opening missed by the dye

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The methylene blue test instils dye directly into the bladder; even small vesicovaginal fistulae allow dye to reach the vaginal swabs. A truly negative result means the bladder-to-vagina pathway is intact, and the leak originates elsewhere.

answers.text: Ureterovaginal fistula

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The methylene blue test checks the bladder-to-vagina pathway. When it is negative but continuous urinary leakage persists, the urine reaches the vagina from the ureter rather than the bladder. The next diagnostic step is the indigo carmine test — intravenous dye excreted by the kidneys — which confirms ureteric origin if it appears in the vagina.

answers.text: Stress urinary incontinence from pelvic floor weakness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stress incontinence occurs in spurts during coughing, sneezing, or exertion — it is not continuous. In a post-hysterectomy patient with constant leakage, a fistula must be excluded through the structured diagnostic sequence before considering other diagnoses.

answers.text: Overactive bladder with urge incontinence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Urge incontinence involves sudden, strong urges with intermittent leakage, not continuous leaking. Continuous post-surgical leakage with a negative methylene blue test points to a ureteric rather than a bladder source — a ureterovaginal fistula.

overallFeedback.feedback: When the methylene blue test (bladder-to-vagina check) is negative but leakage continues, the urine is reaching the vagina from the ureter, not the bladder. This is a ureterovaginal fistula, confirmed by the indigo carmine test (intravenous dye excreted by the kidneys).

Well reasoned. The diagnostic sequence matters: methylene blue tests the bladder first, and if negative, indigo carmine tests the ureter next. This distinction determines the entire surgical approach.

params.question: A woman develops a vesicovaginal fistula following obstructed labour with significant tissue necrosis. When should definitive surgical repair be planned?

answers.text: Within the first 24 hours, before fibrosis sets in

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Early repair (within 72 hours) is appropriate only when tissues are fresh and healthy. In fistulae with significant necrosis and inflammation, operating on damaged tissue leads to repair failure because the fundamental requirement — healthy, well-vascularised tissue margins — is not met.

answers.text: At 2 weeks, once the uterus has involuted

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At 2 weeks, tissue necrosis and inflammatory changes are still active. The tissue is neither soft enough nor well-vascularised enough to hold sutures and heal properly. Adequate time must be allowed for complete tissue recovery.

answers.text: At 3 to 6 months, once tissues are soft and well-vascularised

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When necrosis or inflammation is present, repair is delayed 3 to 6 months. This allows the surrounding tissues to become soft, pliable, and well-vascularised — the fundamental surgical principle underlying every successful fistula repair. The closure must be tension-free with healthy margins.

answers.text: After 12 months, to allow complete pelvic remodelling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While adequate healing time is essential, 12 months is unnecessarily long. The standard recommendation is 3 to 6 months, balancing tissue readiness against the patient's ongoing suffering, social isolation, and loss of dignity from prolonged incontinence.

overallFeedback.feedback: The fundamental rule is tissue condition. With significant necrosis, repair is delayed 3 to 6 months until tissues are soft and well-vascularised. Operating on inflamed or necrotic tissue leads to repair failure. Early repair (within 72 hours) is reserved for cases where tissue is fresh and healthy.

Correct. The timing principle is central: early repair for fresh, healthy tissue; delayed repair (3–6 months) when necrosis or inflammation is present. Successful repair always requires healthy, tension-free, well-vascularised tissue.
